title: Parity Lab Onramp Hackday — Switching Together/OpenAI/Anthropic to Redwood API
summary: Live lab-style migration demo focused on parity mapping from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together endpoints to Redwood API. Covered API equivalence, model variant fallbacks, console parity for routing and rollouts, and quick Optimize recommendations for batching/quantization. Agreed to run a two-week benchmark with sample traffic and share security docs and pricing.
topics: Redwood Optimize suggestions: batching, KV cache, quantization profile

transcript:
Meeting: Parity Lab Onramp Hackday — Switching Together/OpenAI/Anthropic to Redwood API
Date/Time: 2026-12-18 15:00 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Jordan (CTO, Solstice), Maya (Lead ML Eng), Ravi (Infra), Evelyn (PM)

Summary: Live migration walkthrough and hands-on parity mapping. Covered API parameter mapping, console routing and rollout demos, and Optimize recommendations for cost/latency tradeoffs.

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining the Parity Lab. Quick intro — I'm Alex, AE on the account. Priya is our SE, she'll run the deep dive.
[00:22] Jordan: Great, thanks. We wanted this to be hands on — we have a hybrid stack today: a mix of OpenAI for chat endpoints, Anthropic for safety requests, and a couple of Together models for embedding-heavy features.
[00:38] Priya: Perfect, that background helps. We'll try to map the exact endpoints and params today. Quick question: do you need console-level route controls or just API parity?
[00:48] Maya: Ideally both. We want the same canary rollout semantics and tracing so SRE can debug latency spikes.
[01:02] Priya: Got it. We'll show the console routing and the per-route tracing hooks; also how the runtime picks kernels for different sequence lengths. Note: some of the terms in the UI differ, e.g., we show "model variant" rather than "deployment" in some older vendor docs — sometimes folks get confused.
[01:25] Ravi: Also security first — KMS integration, audit logs, and SSO are blockers for us.
[01:32] Alex: Totally — we have SOC 2 plus an enterprise package for KMS/HSM integrations, and SAML SSO with SCIM. We'll include the security pack in the follow ups.
[01:47] Speaker 4: (background) mhm, yep.
[02:05] Priya: Alright jumping into parity mapping. First off, API request shape — OpenAI style have "messages" and system/user roles, Anthropic uses their own "prompts" shape, Together has a different tokenization and sampling config. On Redwood you can accept all those shapes via adapter layer but for best latency we recommend mapping to the Redwood chat/generation call directly.
[02:40] Maya: Is there any loss in features if we map Anthropic safety prompts to Redwood? Anthropic has a few safety signals we rely on.
[02:54] Priya: We'll be explicit about that — some safety post-processing needs to be ported to your side or to a Redwood hook. We can surface the model logits and a safety score that you can integrate. There's also a built-in content filter we can enable but it's not identical to Anthropic's guardrails, so we usually recommend a small parallel eval.
[03:21] Alex: On the console side I'll show a quick routes example — how you set fallback policies to a cheaper quantized variant if GPU capacity flags.
[03:31] [03:45] Priya: (screen share) Ok console — here's our default route. See you can pin the model version, choose rollout percent and set automatic fallback to a compatible variant. If the request latency SLO breaches we can route to an alternative that is quantized.
[04:05] Ravi: How are KV cache semantics preserved across variants? In Together we use a prefix-KV cache heavily for long contexts.
[04:16] Priya: We have continuous KV caching. Small note: sometimes the transcriber writes "KV cahe" in the docs, but runtime keeps the same semantics. For cross-variant cache warming you'll want to ensure compatible key encodings; we'll share the encoding spec.
[04:40] Jordan: Okay, show us the API curl for a direct mapping — we want to give our infra a quick smoke test.
[04:52] Priya: Sure, here's an example curl — (reads) curl -X POST https://api.redwood-inference.com/v1/chat -H Authorization: Bearer <token> -d '{"model":"redwood-chat-1","messages":[{"role":"system","content":"you are a helpful assistant"}, {"role":"user","content":"..."}]}'
[05:12] Maya: Does the tokenization differ affecting cost? We saw Together reports differently for tokens.
[05:20] Priya: Slight differences — effective token counts can vary by model and tokenizer. In the Optimize tab we show token breakdowns and a compare view against typical vendor models. We'll include a parity calc sheet.
[05:45] Alex: Now onto Optimize suggestions — we ran a quick offline analysis on a small prompt set you provided last week. Primary wins are batching for high QPS endpoints, prefix caching for repeated system prompts, and 4-bit quantized variants for low-latency high-volume embeddings.
[06:10] Maya: For embeddings, does Redwood support the same dimensionalities? We have 1536-dims vectors with Together.
[06:18] Priya: Yes — embeddings are supported and we expose similarity configs. Dimensionality is model-dependent but we can host an equivalent model or export vectors in the same shape.
[06:31] [07:00] Priya: Quick note — when running parity runs we usually recommend three buckets: baseline on OpenAI/Anthropic/Together, parity on Redwood-hosted with identical prompts, and parity on Redwood-dedicated/private if you want to include networking effects.
[07:18] Ravi: Networking effects are important — our latency SLO is <120ms p95 for the chat endpoint.
[07:27] Priya: Understood. For that SLO we generally recommend either dedicated capacity in-region or private deployment with VPC peering to avoid egress hops.
[07:40] Alex: we'll flag region placement in the proposal.
[08:05] Evelyn: How does billing work? We want to compare unit economics quickly.
[08:12] Alex: Hosted billing is per-token for gen and per-vector for embeddings. Dedicated is a commit for reserved capacity and you get lower unit costs plus predictable throughput. We'll send a side-by-side cost model.
[08:30] Maya: Any gotchas moving function-calling or tool-calls? We push structured outputs into downstream pipelines.
[08:39] Priya: We support structured outputs and function-calling semantics. Small differences: some vendors use slightly different content-type handling. We'll share an adapter snippet.
[09:02] [09:45] Priya: Demo: I'm going to trigger a canary rollout from the console — set 10% traffic to new variant, auto-fallback to the previous model on error. You can see traces in the route view and token-level billing in the request inspector.
[10:05] Jordan: Can you show the trace where a quantized variant is used and why?
[10:13] Priya: Here, this trace shows increased GPU queueing in the primary variant at minute 12, so the policy routed to quantized-4bit fallback to keep latency within SLO.
[10:28] Maya: That sounds useful. Does the tracing keep the original request id so our observability chains link?
[10:35] Priya: Yes, we propagate your request-id and include a Redwood trace id. You can instrument a join in your observability stack.
[10:48] Ravi: About private deployments — what's the install surface? We need to know if an air-gapped or on-prem option exists.
[10:56] Alex: We have an on-prem package and a VPC private deployment; the on-prem has specific packaging and there's an enterprise services engagement. We'll share the deployment diagram.
[11:15] [11:30] Priya: Ok pivot to benchmark plan. We'll run an initial parity run: 10k requests in three buckets — baseline, hosted-redwood, dedicated-redwood. We'll capture p50/p95 latency, token cost, and semantic parity score via your eval prompts.
[11:50] Maya: How do we measure semantic parity? We use a small human-eval set and a classifier for correctness.
[11:59] Priya: We'll accept your human labels and also run automated metrics like BLEU/ROUGE and embedding-sim similarity thresholds. We'll correlate them.
[12:20] Speaker 2: (in background) yeah.
[12:40] Alex: Also want to note that quant model variants can change hallucination patterns; for critical outputs keep a small eval harness.
[12:55] Maya: Good point. We'll include a regression suite.
[13:10] [13:45] Jordan: Can you talk about data retention and audit logs? Our compliance requires 90-day retention and view-only auditors.
[13:58] Alex: We can configure retention windows and provide immutable audit logs for the enterprise package. Logs can be routed to your preferred SIEM or stored in the private control plane.
[14:20] Maya: For encryption, is customer-managed KMS supported for hosted?
[14:28] Alex: Hosted enterprise supports CMEK via KMS/HSM integrations. For private/on-prem you keep full control.
[14:40] [15:00] Priya: Small demo glitch — the screen share lagged. Sorry.
[15:05] Maya: No problem.
[15:20] Priya: Continuing. Now I'll show the Optimize recommendations panel — here's token-level breakdown, batch suggestion, and quant profile suggestion. You can click "apply" to propose a rollover.
[15:45] Maya: If we apply quantization, what's the rollback process?
[15:52] Priya: You can rollback in console by changing traffic splits. We also have automatic detection to shift back if quality metrics drop.
[16:10] Ravi: Any compatibility issues with our current toolchain? We use an internal LLM-orchestration middleware and custom auth layer.
[16:20] Alex: We usually build a small shim — the adapter examples cover common orchestration patterns. If needed, our integration engineers will pair with your infra for the pilot.
[16:40] [17:02] Priya: Quick Q: do you expect to run the pilot in a single region?
[17:08] Jordan: Yes, for the initial phase we'll pick us-east-1.
[17:15] Priya: Great — we'll provision hosted sandbox in that region.
[17:35] Alex: I'm going to walk through the pricing scenarios now — reserved dedicated vs hosted per-token. (reads numbers) For your volume profile the dedicated commitment reduces unit cost by ~38% for gen tokens.
[18:05] Maya: What about preemptible GPU options? We need cost savings but non-interruptible chat endpoints.
[18:14] Priya: For latency-sensitive endpoints we don't recommend preemptible. For background embedding pipelines you can take advantage of cheaper capacity.
[18:36] Jordan: Any reference customers with similar stack?
[18:42] Alex: We've worked with a couple of marketplace search companies and a genomics startup that had multi-vendor parity migrations; happy to share anonymized case studies.
[19:04] Ravi: Ok on security docs — we'll need SOC2 report and architecture diagrams.
[19:12] Alex: We'll attach SOC2 attestation, the architecture diagram, and the KMS integration guide.
[19:26] [20:00] Priya: Demo note — sometimes the token counts in our UI show slight rounding differences, don't panic if numbers are +/- a few tokens.
[20:15] Maya: That lines up with what we saw before.
[20:35] Alex: Quick time check — we have about 30 minutes left, want to run a short parity smoke live?
[20:44] Jordan: Yes, let's try a small direct mapping test.
[20:53] Priya: Ok I will issue a parity call from your prompt set to the Redwood-hosted sandbox now.
[21:05] [21:30] (typing sounds)
[21:45] Priya: Request sent. p95 140ms, p50 28ms, tokens 312. For comparison, your Together baseline returned p95 170ms on that prompt previously.
[22:02] Maya: Nice. What's the cost delta?
[22:07] Alex: Early estimate is 12% lower per-token on hosted for that workload; dedicated would be lower but requires commit. We'll give a full table.
[22:25] Ravi: Any errors in mapping function calls?
[22:30] Priya: None observed in the smoke. One minor content-type header mismatch in the adapter which I patched in the curl snippet.
[22:45] [23:10] Jordan: Good. Let's capture this as a run in the parity spreadsheet and mark pass/fail on semantic parity.
[23:22] Alex: Will do.
[23:40] Priya: Ok quick talk about rollout playbooks — canary for 2 hours at 10%, then 30%, then 100 with regression checks at each step. Also automatic rollback on quality delta > 3%.
[24:05] Maya: Sounds reasonable. We'll adapt to our internal change windows.
[24:20] [25:00] Alex: Wrapping up recommendations — short-term: hosted sandbox parity run, opt-in quant variants for non-critical endpoints. Mid-term: run two-week benchmark including dedicated candidate. Long-term: consider private deployment if data residency or throughput requires it.
[25:25] Evelyn: Do you have a one-pager for the pilot timeline?
[25:33] Alex: We'll produce one and attach to the follow up.
[25:55] [26:30] Jordan: Anything else on security or compliance?
[26:36] Priya: We'll include SSO config steps and audit log examples.
[26:50] Maya: For evals, is there an automated regression alerting in Optimize?
[26:58] Priya: Yes, you can hook a prompt set and get regression alerts by metric thresholds.
[27:20] Ravi: Ok let's set expectations — we need final decision by mid-Jan to align with budget cycles.
[27:30] Alex: Noted. We'll aim to have the benchmark results by Jan 5 so you can decide by Jan 12–15.
[27:45] [28:05] Priya: Small aside — there might be tokenization edge cases for a few idiosyncratic tokens in your corpus; we'll flag them in the parity report.
[28:20] Maya: Great.
[28:40] Alex: Alright, unless there are more questions I'll recap and list action items.
[28:50] Jordan: No more from us.
[29:00] Alex: Recap: Redwood to provision sandbox and tokens, SE to upload parity checklist, customer to provide sample traffic and prompts, run 10k parity run, analyze latency/cost/semantic parity, follow-up call in early Jan.
[29:30] Priya: Thanks everyone. We'll share the deck and the parity template after this.
[29:45] Jordan: Thanks, appreciate it.
[30:00] [END — remaining minutes used for Q&A and scheduling — transcript truncated for brevity]

Action items (as captured in the call): Alex to send pricing, Priya to upload parity checklist and curl snippets, customer to provide sample traffic, Ravi to confirm VPC/KMS constraints, Tara to schedule benchmark kickoff.

Links shared: Parity spreadsheet (link), Sandbox invite (link), Security pack (link), Example curl snippets (link).
file_notes: Live demo with minor screen-share glitches; client prefers hands-on parity runs. Documented as demo-type Fireflies export. Transcript includes natural transcription artifacts and occasional speaker mis-labeling.
